items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' at the open. He went from 'How are you doing today?' straight into confirming the floors. The closest thing to a roadmap came six minutes in — 'before I go over pricing structure and estimate, do you have any questions any clarification regarding the moving process in general?' — which is a mid-call transition, not a roadmap. The customer never knew how long the call would take or what was coming.

Packing needs never asked. He got a box count ('I doubt it's gonna be more than 25') and learned the customer already bought his own boxes including wardrobe boxes, but never asked whether he wanted packing service on any of it. On a 1BR where the customer is self-packing, that is a live upsell and a real time variable left on the table.

Access concerns never probed on a 20-story high-rise. The customer volunteered the loading dock himself — 'we do have a loading dock but I'm not thinking I'll reserve it since we don't need the truck' — and Arden's reply was to redirect back to the garage/storage question. He never asked whether the freight elevator needs to be reserved, whether the building requires a COI, whether there's a move-in window, or whether the service elevator is shared. On a same-building 14th-to-20th-floor move, elevator access is the single biggest time variable and it went completely unexamined after the customer opened the door to it.

No Worries Damage Coverage was mis-branded. 'you're going to get up to $2,000 free evaluation coverage. So, if anything gets damaged gets broken, you can just give us a call to file a claim for it.' The $2,000 and the free landed; the brand name did not, 'repair, replace, or reimburse' did not, and the 60¢/lb industry baseline it is supposed to be measured against never came up — so the customer has no way to know the coverage is unusual.

Disassembly/reassembly time never factored into the estimate. He covered a marble-top dresser, two marble nightstands, a heavy solid-wood desk, a headboard/footboard/rails bed, and two wall-mounted TVs the customer will dismount himself — then quoted 2.5 to 3 hours without ever saying how much of that is teardown and rebuild time. The tools being included was stated; the hours being consumed was not.

No 'reply with any corrections' on the confirmation email. What he said was 'I already sent you the confirmation email. You can run through it everything that we have discussed is on, is on there, okay?' — that invites reading, not verifying. On a call where unit numbers were captured by ear ('It's 14061406' → 1406, and '2002' which the customer echoed back as '202'), an explicit correction ask is the cheapest possible insurance against a crew showing up at the wrong door.
BOLDED key details at the top of the email never mentioned.
Hours and how to reach us never given. 'all you need to do is just give us a call' was said twice with no number and no hours attached.

Effective insurance framing missed — no 60¢/lb baseline, no comparison, no explanation of what a claim actually looks like, on a move carrying a marble-top dresser and two marble nightstands, which are exactly the items that chip.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. No 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill,' no consolidation examples, no carload tip, no 'does that make sense?' close. This was a strong candidate for it: same building, up six floors, with a one-school-bus walk at the origin and a two-school-bus walk at the destination. Every loose item the customer walks over himself in the week before is billable time at $333/hour with a three-mover crew.
top_strength: Arden's discovery on the heavy items is the best piece of estimate-accuracy work in this week's sample, and he did it without being asked. When the customer said 'I have a safe. I don't know the dimensions,' Arden didn't accept it and move on — he pushed three separate times: 'How much does the safe weigh do you think?', 'Is it heavier than £300?', and then 'if you can give me the make and model, it's okay if you can give me the make and model of the safe if you can check on it right now. So we can double-check and Google the weight.' He then named the actual operational reason out loud — 'at least, we'll know whether the movers, we really need three movers for this or it's just two movers' — and when the customer went digging through Amazon order history, Arden held the line warmly: 'It's okay sir, you take your time. I'm just here.' The answer came back at 86 lbs. That is a rep chasing a real number instead of guessing, on exactly the input that drives crew size. He used the same discipline on walk distance, and the school-bus equivalent did real work: 'we can measure it using a school bus. Is it one school bus away or half a school bus away from this elevator?' got him a usable number where 'it's not far and it's about halfway along the floor' had not. He then repeated it at the destination and correctly inferred the layout — 'Oh, so you're at the end of the hallway for the second department' — confirmed by the customer. Second strength: he handled the price-versus-online-quote objection cleanly and without discounting. 'So am I better off doing the quote online or cause I, it was an $830' got a direct, factual reconciliation — 'The $832 is a two and a half hour minimum for three movers. It's $999 estimate for two and a half to three hours' — and the customer's reply was 'I got it. I got it. Okay, I got it. That's how I didn't know how you did the [quote] online. I understand that.' He followed it with a value reframe that named the objection before the customer could: 'our hourly rate might sound higher than what our competitors has but come to think of it everything that we have are all already transparent. We don't have hidden fees. We don't surprise you with transportation fees.' The customer answered 'I know there's some places that have a cheaper rate per hour, but I don't think they do the right service' and booked. Pricing section is 19/20 and he hit both Meet Your Mover and the On-Time Guarantee — the two differentiators the company-wide numbers say almost nobody hits.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: the Save Your Ass speech is a flat zero on a call that was otherwise a 63. Arden already established that the walk is one school bus at the origin and two school buses at the destination — he has the customer's own numbers to build the pitch on. The line was sitting right there: 'Mark, one more thing that saves you real money. You're in the same building, so anything small and awkward — the loose stuff in drawers, the closet odds and ends, the pictures off the walls, the wardrobe boxes once they're full — carry those up yourself in the week before, or take a cartload at a time. With three movers at $333 an hour, every fifteen minutes they aren't walking two school buses with a box is real money back in your pocket. Does that make sense?' That is a ten-point section and, on a two-school-bus hallway, it is the highest-dollar advice on the entire call. Second priority: the elevator. The customer volunteered the loading dock unprompted and Arden steered away from it. On a 14th-to-20th-floor move inside one building, whether the freight elevator is reserved and for how long is the difference between a three-hour move and a five-hour move, and it is a question the customer can answer with one call to his leasing office. Add it to the access block permanently: 'Does your building require you to reserve the service elevator, and do they need a certificate of insurance from us?' Third, fix the coverage naming — 'up to $2,000 free evaluation coverage' should be 'No Worries Damage Coverage — up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage,' and pair it with the 60¢/lb industry baseline. He is moving a marble-top dresser and two marble nightstands; that is the exact customer who needs to hear what the coverage actually does. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review: Arden committed to three movers before the safe was resolved, then justified the crew size after the fact with the safe still in the list — 'since we have, we do have some heavy items, heavy marble items and some heavy, solid wood desk. And you also have a safe, it's good to do three movers.' By that point the safe had been established at 86 lbs, well under the 300 lb limit he himself had cited, so it was no longer a reason for anything. The marble pieces and the two-school-bus walk may well justify three movers on their own, but the stated rationale included an input that had already been ruled out, and the result was $999 against the system's $832 — a 20% increase over the online quote on a same-building 1BR. He also said 'we only factored in a little extra time in this quote,' which is honest padding language but padding language nonetheless. This one is worth pulling the actual against on 9/25: if three movers finish in 2.5 hours, the call was right; if two movers would have done it in three, the crew upgrade cost the customer roughly $170. Last, close the email loop with a verification ask. He sent the confirmation but never said 'read it over and reply if anything's off' — and he captured both unit numbers by ear on a call where the customer echoed back '202' for unit 2002.
phone_presence_notes: Genuine, patient warmth throughout — 'It's okay sir, you take your time. I'm just here' while the customer dug through Amazon orders, a gracious recovery when the customer misheard the garage question ('Oh. Oh, I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' → 'It's okay.'), the customer's name used four times, and a farewell with real character ('bye-bye mark. Stay safe. Happy weekend') — held back from a 5 only by a long, clearly scripted pricing block that ran without a check-in and a string of bare 'Mm-hmm' acknowledgments during the item inventory.
audio_review_reason: The clarity-and-pace bullet was deducted on transcript evidence that is unusually unreliable here. The transcript garbles a high proportion of this rep's speech — 'no sare. Fees', 'Ansin moving', 'word of amount', 'helping extension of changers arriving at your Fri[ont door]', 'Holiwood' for solid wood, and the estimate rendered as '$9, okay, $999' — which could be a genuinely fast or accented delivery the customer struggled with, or could be transcription artifact on clear speech. The customer asked for a repeat only once ('You said I want them into the minimum. How many hours?'), which points to the latter, but audio is needed to settle it before this is coached as a pace issue.
